system_prompt:
You are taking part in a measurement benchmark. You will see an image of a
single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) strip. Your job is to read waveform timing
from the image as precisely as you can. This is not a diagnostic task.
user_prompt:
The image shows Lead II of a 10-second ECG recording. The horizontal axis
is time in seconds measured from the start of the recording (0.0 s at the left
edge, 10.0 s at the right edge). The vertical axis is voltage in millivolts (mV).
Major grid lines are every 0.2 s and 0.5 mV; minor grid lines are every 0.04 s
and 0.1 mV.

Task: list the time of the peak of every QRS complex in Lead II whose peak
falls inside the scoring window 3.0 s to 7.0 s (the
shaded region). For each QRS complex, mark the top of its upward (positive)
deflection, the R wave, even when that upward part is small compared with a
downward part. Narrow vertical pacemaker spikes are not QRS peaks.

Report times in seconds from the start of the recording (not relative to the
window), as decimal numbers. Include every QRS peak in the window and nothing
else (no P waves, T waves, or artifacts).

Respond with only this JSON object and no other text:
{"qrs_peaks_s": [<time in seconds>, ...]}

raw_response:
Looking at the zoomed views:

**3.0–5.0 s:** Two QRS complexes — one with R peak just right of the 3.8 line (~3.83 s), and one just left of the 4.8 line (~4.75 s).

**5.0–7.0 s:** Two QRS complexes — one just right of the 5.6 line (~5.65 s), and one just left of the 6.6 line (~6.57 s).

The QRS complexes occur at a regular spacing (~0.91 s), consistent with peaks at ~0.3, 1.2, 2.1, 2.9, 3.83, 4.75, 5.65, 6.57, 7.5, 8.4, 9.35 s. The complex at ~2.9 s lies outside the window (before 3.0 s), and the next falls after 7.0 s.

raw_response:
Looking at the strip, the rhythm is regular with an RR interval of about 0.4 s (≈150 bpm). The first QRS peak occurs at about 0.2 s, and peaks continue at roughly 0.4 s intervals (approximately 0.2, 0.6, 1.0, 1.4, ... s).

Within the scoring window 3.0–7.0 s, the visible R-wave peaks fall at approximately:

- just after the 3.0 s line (~3.0–3.05 s)
- ~3.4 s
- ~3.8 s
- ~4.2 s
- ~4.6 s
- ~5.0 s
- ~5.4 s
- ~5.8 s
- ~6.2 s
- ~6.6 s

The next peak falls just after the 7.0 s boundary (≈7.0–7.1 s), so it is outside the window, and no peak falls before 3.0 s inside the window. Each of these is a tall positive R wave in Lead II, with no pacemaker spikes present.

{"qrs_peaks_s": [3.04, 3.44, 3.84, 4.24, 4.64, 5.04, 5.44, 5.84, 6.24, 6.64]}

is time in seconds measured from the start of the recording (0.0 s at the left
edge, 10.0 s at the right edge). The vertical axis is voltage in millivolts (mV).
Major grid lines are every 0.2 s and 0.5 mV; minor grid lines are every 0.04 s
and 0.1 mV.

Task: list the time of the peak of every QRS complex in Lead II whose peak
falls inside the scoring window 3.0 s to 7.0 s (the
shaded region). For each QRS complex, mark the top of its upward (positive)
deflection, the R wave, even when that upward part is small compared with a
downward part. Narrow vertical pacemaker spikes are not QRS peaks.

Report times in seconds from the start of the recording (not relative to the
window), as decimal numbers. Include every QRS peak in the window and nothing
else (no P waves, T waves, or artifacts).

Respond with only this JSON object and no other text:
{"qrs_peaks_s": [<time in seconds>, ...]}

raw_response:
Looking at the strip, I need to locate the R-wave peaks within the shaded scoring window (3.0–7.0 s).

Mapping the time axis: 0.0 s at the left edge (~x=137 px) to 10.0 s at the right edge (~x=2357 px), giving ~222 px per second. Major grid lines every 0.2 s.

Identifying the QRS complexes (sharp upward deflections) across the strip:
- ~0.3 s, ~1.4 s, ~2.3 s (before the window)
- ~3.35 s (inside window, just after 3.0 s line)
- ~4.40 s (inside window, about 0.4 s after 4.0 s line)
- ~5.25 s (inside window, about 0.25 s after 5.0 s line)
- ~6.15 s (inside window, about 0.15 s after 6.0 s line)
- ~7.05 s (just past the right edge of the shaded window, at the 7.0 s boundary — excluded)
- ~7.95 s, ~8.85 s (after the window)

Checking each candidate against the window boundaries: the peaks at ~3.35, ~4.40, ~5.25, and ~6.15 s clearly fall inside the shaded 3.0–7.0 s region. The next peak sits just outside the 7.0 s boundary, so it is excluded. No other QRS peaks fall in the window.

Final times: 3.35, 4.4, 5.25, 6.15 s.

{"qrs_peaks_s": [3.35, 4.4, 5.25, 6.15]}

system_prompt:
You are taking part in a measurement benchmark. You will see an image of a
single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) strip. Your job is to read waveform timing
from the image as precisely as you can. This is not a diagnostic task.
user_prompt:
The image shows Lead II of a 10-second ECG recording. The horizontal axis
is time in seconds measured from the start of the recording (0.0 s at the left
edge, 10.0 s at the right edge). The vertical axis is voltage in millivolts (mV).
Major grid lines are every 0.2 s and 0.5 mV; minor grid lines are every 0.04 s
and 0.1 mV.

Task: list the time of the peak of every QRS complex in Lead II whose peak
falls inside the scoring window 3.0 s to 7.0 s (the
shaded region). For each QRS complex, mark the top of its upward (positive)
deflection, the R wave, even when that upward part is small compared with a
downward part. Narrow vertical pacemaker spikes are not QRS peaks.

Report times in seconds from the start of the recording (not relative to the
window), as decimal numbers. Include every QRS peak in the window and nothing
else (no P waves, T waves, or artifacts).

Respond with only this JSON object and no other text:
{"qrs_peaks_s": [<time in seconds>, ...]}

Looking at the image, I need to identify each QRS complex (R wave peak) within the shaded scoring window from 3.0 s to 7.0 s.

**Reading the grid:** The x-axis runs from 0.0 s (left edge) to 10.0 s (right edge), with major grid lines every 0.2 s and minor lines every 0.04 s. The scoring window 3.0–7.0 s is shaded.

**Locating the QRS complexes:** Scanning the strip, the R waves (tall upward spikes) occur at fairly regular intervals of about 0.78–0.80 s. The spikes visible in or near the window are:

- A spike just after the 3.0 s line, at roughly 3.5 s (between the 3.4 and 3.6 grid lines).
- A spike at about 4.3 s (between 4.2 and 4.4).
- A spike just after the 5.0 s line, at about 5.1 s.
- A spike just before the 6.0 s line, at about 5.9 s.
- A spike between the 6.6 and 6.8 lines, at about 6.7 s.

The next spike falls at about 7.4 s (outside the window), and the previous one at about 2.7 s (also outside). So exactly five QRS peaks fall inside the scoring window.

**Checking each candidate:** All five spikes are narrow, sharp upward deflections typical of R waves, clearly distinct from the broader, lower P and T waves and from any pacing artifacts. Their amplitudes vary slightly (the beats near 4.3–5.1 s are a bit smaller), but the top of the upward deflection is unambiguous in each case.

**Refining times:** Using the major gridlines (0.2 s spacing) as anchors:
- Peak 1: ~3.5 s (slightly past the 3.4 line)
- Peak 2: ~4.3 s
- Peak 3: ~5.1 s (just after the 5.0 line)
- Peak 4: ~5.9 s (just before the 6.0 line)
- Peak 5: ~6.7 s

These give consistent R–R intervals of ~0.78–0.80 s, matching the rest of the strip.

single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) strip. Your job is to read waveform timing
from the image as precisely as you can. This is not a diagnostic task.
user_prompt:
The image shows Lead II of a 10-second ECG recording. The horizontal axis
is time in seconds measured from the start of the recording (0.0 s at the left
edge, 10.0 s at the right edge). The vertical axis is voltage in millivolts (mV).
Major grid lines are every 0.2 s and 0.5 mV; minor grid lines are every 0.04 s
and 0.1 mV.

Task: list the time of the peak of every QRS complex in Lead II whose peak
falls inside the scoring window 3.0 s to 7.0 s (the
shaded region). For each QRS complex, mark the top of its upward (positive)
deflection, the R wave, even when that upward part is small compared with a
downward part. Narrow vertical pacemaker spikes are not QRS peaks.

Report times in seconds from the start of the recording (not relative to the
window), as decimal numbers. Include every QRS peak in the window and nothing
else (no P waves, T waves, or artifacts).

Respond with only this JSON object and no other text:
{"qrs_peaks_s": [<time in seconds>, ...]}

Time labels in zoomed views use the same origin as the full image. You may
call it at most 6 times. When you are done, give your final answer
as the JSON object.

raw_response:
Looking at the strip, I identify the QRS complexes by their tall, sharp upward deflections (R waves), which occur at roughly regular intervals of about 1.05–1.1 s:

- ~0.75 s (outside window, before 3.0 s)
- ~1.8 s (outside window)
- ~2.9 s (just before the 3.0 s window edge – excluded)
- ~4.0 s (inside window)
- ~5.2 s (inside window)
- ~6.3 s (inside window)
- ~7.4 s (just after the 7.0 s window edge – excluded)
- ~8.5 s, ~9.5 s (outside window)

The small narrow spikes (e.g., near 5.1 s) are pacemaker artifacts, not QRS peaks, and the rounded bumps are P and T waves, so they are not counted.

Checking the window boundaries: the QRS at ~2.9 s peaks before the shaded region begins at 3.0 s, and the QRS at ~7.4 s peaks after the shaded region ends at 7.0 s. Thus only three QRS peaks fall inside the scoring window: at approximately 4.0 s, 5.2 s, and 6.3 s.

{"qrs_peaks_s": [4.0, 5.2, 6.3]}
